extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, accurate, and interesting news sentences, choosing precise words, and reporting interviews/speeches (leads, fairness, coherence, handling conversation, etc.) aimed at reporters producing news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentials of the Sentence — accuracy and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A good sentence must possess two essentials: accuracy and interest. Accuracy is primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy: coordinate and subordinate parts correctly; give pronouns definite antecedents; keep verbs consistent and agreeing in person and number; make effective use of ellipsis. Interest: make sentences clear and forceful by keeping grammatically connected words/phrases/clauses close together; eliminate lengthy parenthetic expressions; avoid unnecessary shifts of subject within sentences; make relations between phrases clear; put important ideas at the beginning and end of the sentence; make sentences short and concise; acquire delicacy of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words — accuracy and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: For words as for sentences, the twin laws are accuracy and interest: words must be accurate in meaning and stimulate reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in word choice (precise diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always write with regard for exact shades of meaning — search for the single noun, verb, or adjective that best expresses an idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid looseness of thinking and inexact expressions. Never be content with a near word; avoid tricks or buffoonery to evade difficulty. Example: misuse of 'lurid' (precise meaning pale yellow, wan, ghastly) shows common inaccuracy. The text provides an extensive list of commonly confused/misused word pairs (e.g., above/over; last/latest; affect/effect; less/fewer; etc.) which reporters should distinguish keenly and avoid misusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness of words (simplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure interest, words must be clear and forceful; avoid technical, ornate, or little-known words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple, everyday Anglo-Saxon words (home vs. residence, begin vs. commence). The average newspaper reader has a limited vocabulary; ornate diction injures a story. A list of inflated words and the simpler replacements is provided (e.g., aggregate → total; inaugurate → begin; casket → coffin; commence → begin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Force (specificity and aptness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words should be emphatic, fitting, apt, fresh, and specific rather than general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific terms to vague ones (e.g., 'ten thousand persons' instead of 'a vast concourse' or 'about ten thousand'). Omit 'about' when a specific figure suffices; use specific numbers and concrete terms to increase force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding trite phrases (originality of expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest requires originality and avoidance of hackneyed or trite phraseology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters must find new ways to tell recurring human events; avoid clichés like 'tripped the light fantastic', 'the bride was elegantly gowned', etc. Strive for fresh, sparkling expression every day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figures of speech — tasteful and coherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of speech add suggestiveness and interpretation but must be used cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They can make prose more effective (figurative vs. literal), but avoid mixing metaphors or creating ridiculous images. Do not personify ships, cities, states, or countries. Example of mixed figure to avoid is given. Use figures only when apt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance and good usage (attention to usage details)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe minor usage conventions and etiquette of titles and forms to maintain elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: refer to a minister as 'the Rev. Mr. Anderson', not 'Rev. Anderson'; do not invent titles (e.g., 'Railway Inspector Brown' if unnecessary). Avoid the overused editorial 'we' in unsigned stories; avoid stilted or archaic self-references (the scribe, your humble servant). In signed stories, 'I' may be used more freely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slang — limited and context-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Slang is barred from most columns because it lacks elegance and clearness, though it may be acceptable on sporting pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slang is often regionally or socially limited and may be unintelligible to wide readership; news stories are for heterogeneous audiences, so avoid slang. Newly coined words may be admitted, but when in doubt consult a standard dictionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of basic news story types
rubrics_metrics.description: For a beginner, most news stories reduce to a limited set: interviews; accidents; society; sports; plus rewrites, feature stories, and correspondence stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grouping helps reporters learn handling methods; interviews, speeches, courts, meetings, conventions, banquets, official reports, and stories about articles/books are similar in handling (grouped under interview type).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads to an interview — feature choices
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead to an interview may feature: (1) the name of the person interviewed, (2) a direct statement from him, (3) an indirect statement, (4) the general topic, (5) the occasion, or (6) the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most often the name or a direct statement is featured. If using the name, locate conversation in time/place and possibly include a direct/indirect quote or summary. If a significant statement is key, start with that statement and follow with speaker name, time, place, and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements of local interest — lead with local relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, lead by getting the interviewee to express opinion about a topic of local interest and feature that statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask about civic, state, or national issues that matter locally; feature such opinions especially when they align with paper policy. For prominent national figures, ask their view on issues of national importance to make the lead locally relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiring about the feature — ask interviewee what to bring out
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, ask the person interviewed if there is anything he wishes brought out or developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a courtesy. Do not submit copy for the interviewee's criticism before publication except in extraordinary circumstances — doing so often ruins the story's piquancy and may lead to repudiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in the interview — accuracy and absence of bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The interviewer must aim for fairness, accuracy, and absence of personal bias; the interview should not be used as an unfair weapon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to color a person's opinions; avoid editorializing in the interview. You may break into quoted paragraphs to explain or elaborate, or obtain and quote a reply from a local figure if the speaker's assertions need challenge or balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and proportion in interview copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reorder and proportion ideas logically so the printed interview presents thought and spirit coherently, regardless of how they were spoken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regroup material when interviewees give disproportionate attention to minor points or drift off topic; ensure the sequence and proportion of ideas are logical for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying the one interviewed — establish authority and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide explanation about who the interviewee is and how the interview was obtained to give readers necessary context and confidence in his statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief biographical or positional detail (rank, reputation, relevant past acts) helps readers know why the speaker's views are worth attention; many readers may not recognize prominent names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling conversation — condense and quote selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Condense prolix parts of conversation; quote exact language where interest rests in how something was said; avoid reproducing everything verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut to the bone: give pithy summaries for dull or wordy parts and return to direct quotation when the speaker is interesting. Avoid a dry Q&A format; instead create sparkling personal paragraphs with direct statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mannerisms and description to liven interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpolate bits of description and mannerisms (pet phrases, gestures, sudden anger, reticence) to present atmosphere and spirit of the interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-placed incidental details can be as effective as extended quotations in conveying personality and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons refusing to talk — report the foiled interview
rubrics_metrics.description: If a subject refuses to talk or you fail to make him talk, you can still produce a good story by narrating foiled efforts or quoting the questions refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful observation of demeanor, evasions, and surrounding circumstances can yield a newsworthy narrative (example: foiled interview of Secretary Bryan providing premonitory details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of inference in foiled interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful reporter uses rare judgment and inference to build a story from few facts, noting small incidents that suggest larger events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study examples of foiled interviews to learn how to play up few details and infer likely developments; knowing people and men helps produce scoops where cub reporters would get nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of interviews — lead and paragraph structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story contains many interviews, lead with the consensus of opinion, then present individual quotations with names prominent at paragraph starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For many interviews, consider display type for names; if interviewees are not prominent but their statements are valuable, give quotations successively and bury names within paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leads for speeches — many acceptable approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: A speech lead may feature: (1) the speaker's theme, (2) the title of the address, (3) a forceful direct quotation, (4) an indirect quotation of dynamic statements, (5) the speaker's name, (6) the occasion, or (7) the time/place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the approach according to what is most important in the address. Use subject/title when particularly apt; use a single-sentence quotation to give the keynote when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featuring a single sentence or paragraph in the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: A single direct quotation that gives the keynote of a speech or harmonizes with paper policy makes an effective lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a quotation that encapsulates the address and follow with necessary context (speaker, place, occasion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Playing up random statements when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a random statement can be used as a lead if it aligns with a paper's policy or serves as an unprejudiced feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statements are valuable because they appear unmotivated; however, always make clear the relation of the featured quote to the speech as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect quotation to shift emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use indirect quotation in the lead to shift an important point to the very first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirectly phrasing a speaker's point allows placing the key idea up front while reserving direct quotes for later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title or theme featured in speech leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature the title or the theme of the speech when either is particularly expressive or captures the address's nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the subject if it is especially happy or gives the essence (e.g., 'The National Importance of Woman's Health'). If no single sentence is available and the title doesn't indicate nature, feature the theme.
